heroText: Ouagadougou, known locally as Ouaga, is Burkina Faso's sprawling capital and its administrative, cultural and economic centre on the West African Sahel. First-time visitors should browse the Musée National du Burkina Faso for regional history, watch the weekly ceremony at the Moro-Naba Palace, and shop for masks and bronze work at the Village Artisanal de Ouagadougou. Thomas Sankara International Airport sits close to the centre, a short ride from most hotels.

areas.name: Koulouba
areas.text: Koulouba is the historic administrative district near the centre, home to the presidential palace and within easy reach of the National Museum.

areas.name: Zone du Bois
areas.text: Zone du Bois is a leafy, planned residential area popular with expatriates, known for its parks and quieter, tree-lined streets.

areas.name: Ouaga 2000
areas.text: Ouaga 2000 is the city's modern, upscale district of embassies, government buildings and newer hotels, best for business travellers needing space.

airports.name: Thomas Sankara International Airport (OUA)
airports.search: Thomas Sankara International Airport, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso
airports.text: Thomas Sankara International Airport sits about 3 kilometres from the city centre, making transfers quick, though it's worth confirming pickup for late flights.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between Thomas Sankara International Airport (OUA) and central Ouagadougou before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

stayOverview: Base in Koulouba for walking access to the National Museum and government district, or choose Zone du Bois for a quieter, leafy stay. Ouaga 2000 suits business travellers who want modern hotels near the embassies and more space.
hotelIntro: Hotel choice in Ouagadougou depends on purpose: Koulouba keeps history and government sights within reach, Zone du Bois offers calmer expatriate-favoured streets, and Ouaga 2000 provides the city's newest hotels close to embassies and business offices.
rentalCars: A rental car or hired driver helps for reaching Ouaga 2000 and out-of-town sites, though taxis cover the compact central districts well.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose Koulouba for walking access to the National Museum and central sights, or Ouaga 2000 for newer business-friendly hotels.

travelTips.title: Getting around
travelTips.text: Agree taxi fares before setting off, since meters are rarely used, and keep small notes on hand for short rides.

travelTips.title: Moro-Naba ceremony
travelTips.text: Time a Friday morning visit to see the traditional ceremony at the Moro-Naba Palace, a rare glimpse of pre-colonial ritual still performed today.

travelTips.title: Day trips
travelTips.text: Set aside half a day for the sacred crocodile pond at Bazoulé, a short drive from the city and a memorable wildlife stop.

highlights.title: Place des Cineastes
highlights.text: Place des Cineastes is a named stop in Ouagadougou worth keeping on the route when it fits the day's transport, timing and neighborhood plan.

highlights.title: National Museum of Burkina Faso
highlights.text: National Museum of Burkina Faso is a key Ouagadougou culture stop, useful for understanding local history, collections and rainy-day planning near the main sightseeing route.

highlights.title: Ouagadougou Cathedral
highlights.text: Ouagadougou Cathedral anchors the historic and ceremonial side of Ouagadougou, making it a practical stop for architecture, local memory and orientation.

highlights.title: Bangr-Weoogo Urban Park
highlights.text: Bangr-Weoogo Urban Park adds outdoor time to a Ouagadougou stay, with open space, views or waterfront breathing room between denser city sights.

highlights.title: Moro-Naba Palace
highlights.text: Moro-Naba Palace anchors the historic and ceremonial side of Ouagadougou, making it a practical stop for architecture, local memory and orientation.

highlights.title: Grand Market of Ouagadougou
highlights.text: Grand Market of Ouagadougou gives Ouagadougou a concrete street-life stop, with food, everyday shopping and local movement that helps visitors read the city.

nearbyIdeas.name: Bazoulé
nearbyIdeas.label: Wildlife
nearbyIdeas.text: Bazoulé is a village near Ouagadougou famous for its sacred crocodile pond, where visitors can see crocodiles up close in a traditional setting.

nearbyIdeas.name: Laongo Sculpture Symposium
nearbyIdeas.label: Art
nearbyIdeas.text: The Laongo Sculpture Symposium site displays large granite sculptures carved into natural rock outcrops, a striking open-air gallery outside the city.

Foundation and regional importance Ouagadougou was founded possibly as early as 1050 by the Soninke Wangara diaspora from the Ghana Empire, also known as Wagadu.

history.label: 14th century
history.text: The Mossi people, moving north in the 14th century, conquered Wagadugu around the same time they raided Walata, contributing to the decline of the Mali Empire.

history.label: 15th century
history.text: The eponymous Wagadugu Kingdom was founded in the 15th century, which became the main center of the Mossi States around 1495.

history.label: 17th century
history.text: The 10th Moro Naba, Nyadfo, was the first Moro-Naba to live at Ouagadougou, in the middle of the 17th century.
On 5 September 1896 French forces entered Ouagadougou and burned the city to the ground.
In 1919 the colonial administration made Ouagadougou the capital of the Upper Volta territory, extensively rebuilding the town.

In 1954 the railroad line from Ivory Coast reached the city, spurring massive population growth. Independence On 15 January 2016, gunmen armed with heavy weapons attacked central Ouagadougou at the Cappuccino restaurant and the.

history.label: Civic role
history.text: According to legend, the city was taken by Oubri, a grandson of Ouedraogo.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: It became the permanent capital under the 21st Moro Naba, Zombre, a century later.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: The Moro-Naba Ceremony is still performed every Friday by the Moro-Naba and his court.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: The 24th Moro Naba, Doulougou, built the first mosque in Ouagadougou early in the nineteenth century.
